rv.q: If “Stranger Things: The First Shadow” offers brainless theme-park jump-scares, “Bug”’s bold imagery, especially as the story hurdles toward its end, provokes raw terror.
She’s magnificent onstage, returning to Broadway for the first time since Steppenwolf’s 2012 revival of “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?”
Smallwood, who is not well known in New York, will be a revelation to many.
In the director David Cromer’s spare, intelligent production, the set hovers inside an inky blackness.
This revival announces “Bug” as a layered and assured tragedy for our cracked moment.
Manic, disturbing and relentless, "Bug" gets under the audience’s skin and remains there long after the final curtain drops.
The slipperiness of ostensible skepticism into utter credulity is what makes Bug continue to resonate so powerfully today.
Letts and his director and their cast don't take us in hand as they descend into the madness

Despite the cesspits of ­conspiracy-think that pollute contemporary politics, the specific paranoia of Letts’s ­characters — bugs under the skin, brainwashing, ­nefarious doctors in government labs — feels less blazingly relevant than comparatively quaint.
But when Peter thinks he notices a bug bite from their shared motel bed, he starts to spiral further into paranoia.
Bug is the scariest play ever written.
It goes without saying that "Bug" belongs to Coon, whose transfixing tour de force is reason enough to snap up a ticket immediately.
It affirms the play’s stature as a major work of dramatic literature and is a stimulating and wrenching theatrical experience.

Even as his characters destroy their world and themselves, Letts never loses sight of the strange comfort in a good conspiracy theory. (Many of the real-life examples Peter manically cites are, in fact, entirely true.) One unifying theory making sense of all the pain is, for these damaged souls, so much more comforting.

When Bug was first seen Off-Broadway in 2004, it seemed prescient in its portrayal of mental illness and conspiracy theories. Now — after the world has gone collectively crazy with wacky notions about COVID, pedophile rings, vaccines, and 5G, among countless other things — Tracy Letts’ play practically feels quaint.
Letts, who often thinks the worst of his characters and is rarely wrong, offers an alarmingly mordant comment on the current paranoid style of American life.
Between fine acting and the chance to see a seldom-represented genre on stage, theatregoers have reasons to swarm to Bug.
Instead, this “Bug” is intelligent, disciplined, and often absorbing—but rarely electrifying.
But it’s better appreciated as a live‑wire artifact of a writer finding his voice and seeing what buttons he could push.
That is a truth that rings throughout the production, and it includes those of us in the audience as well.
David Cromer's leisurely direction turns this into a character study instead
Bug’s bite seems shallower than I recall.
But Bug doesn’t find a way to deepen this journey to hell, merely to repeat it—or find a useful purpose for the characters of R.C. and Jerry; both become under-utilized foils.
Much of the effect for me has worn off.
Unfortunately, very little of that tension actually exists on stage.
Hard as she tries, Coon just seems too intelligent at her core to fall for Peter’s far-fetched tale, no matter how desperate she is for “love” and companionship.
Bug is a true masterpiece, and its spellbinding storytelling is cinematic and absorbing.
That choice speaks volumes about how seductive shared madness can be when the alternative is isolation.
Carrie Coon and Namir Smallwood deliver performances that get under your skin in Tracy Letts' paranoid, unsettling Broadway debut of Bug.

As Lett’s taut story builds to its tense and graphic denouement, you begin to sense how Bug has emerged as both an acute psychological study of two damaged people inflicting damage on each other and also a parable for our age of heightened, often tribal paranoia.
Coon, who hasn’t been on Broadway since her debut in 2012, is the real deal and will keep you on your toes, as will set design Takeshi Kata’s mind-blowing scene change late in the play.
Bug lives or dies on the sexual and neurotic chemistry of its two leads, and if half the equation is muted, terror lapses into bathos.
That fundamental misreading drains the play of its devastating impact.
I found myself observing how well they were crafting their performances rather than being moved by them.

cn.t: Tracy Letts' paranoid thriller receives a visceral Broadway debut with Carrie Coon delivering a powerhouse performance. Critics praise its unsettling relevance to today's conspiracy-minded culture, though some find the pacing uneven and the premise dated.
